chapter_theme: Two songs at Madambakkam (மாடம்பாக்கம்) on the courtesans: their charms one by one, and the whole cycle of the bargain, the bed, the robbery, the beating and the new man; the poet asks to be ruled at the lotus feet, and the praise names Murugan as the light of the Agamas beyond maya and as teacher of Siva.

701.reading: The poet lists the charms of the price-women one by one, earrings, bangled hands, voice like the yazh, smile, scented hair, honeyed lips, wide eyes, anklets, rose water and breasts, and asks Murugan whether he will not think to rule him at the lotus feet with anklets, so that he does not tire, sunk in infatuation through their wiles. The praise names Murugan as the light hard to reach that the Sivagamas proclaim, the form of nada, tantra and kala, the one sought by the four Vedas, beyond maya, who brings the stilling of the mind, the hero whose vel cut down Sura, and the teacher who, when Siva said 'tell it', spoke the dawn of the bliss of knowledge, at Madaiyampathi.
701.nuance: The first half repeats ஆலே, 'by', after each charm, a catalogue that ends in விலைமாதர் பாவகங்கள், the price-women's feigned feelings. The praise is unusually doctrinal: சிவாகமங்கள், நாத தந்த்ர கலா, மாயாதீத, மனோலயம். கூறென அரனார் முன் ... ஞானசுகோதயம் புகல் தேசிக: Murugan teaching Siva, without naming Om.

702.reading: The poet tells the courtesans' whole routine: setting the price, hiding the breasts, loosening the hair, darting eyes, twisting speech, standing out in the open, accosting rough men and following them, saying 'isn't it wrong to turn back after taking the betel?', taking them to bed, then snatching all their wealth, quarrelling and beating them away, and taking up a new man with new stories; he asks whether Murugan will rule him, a great sinner unshaken even after seeing their ways, who lacks the knowledge to approach the fragrant feet even for a moment. The praise names Siva, struck with a bow, who cut off Brahma's middle head and begged with it and burned the triple city with a smile, with Uma at his side, sounds the battle in drum syllables, names Rama who cut Ravana's ten heads and twenty arms with one arrow, and Murugan who comes on the peacock, the young lord of a golden town amid pearl-strewn fields.
702.nuance: The routine runs from விலையறுக்கவும், fixing the price, to புதிய பேருடனே கதைகள் செப்பவும், the next customer, a full cycle of the trade. குணங்கண்டும் துளங்கா: the poet's fault is that seeing it all does not shake him. The song ends with இளைய நாயகனே rather than பெருமாளே and names the town only as தமனியப்பதி, the golden town.

links.note: Both tell the courtesan's cycle to its end, the man welcomed while his wealth lasts and then beaten and driven out; 702 adds the bargaining at the start and the new man taken up afterwards.

701 lists the price-women's charms one by one, among them the voice like the yazh (யாழ்தரு கீத மென்குரல்), and ends in their feigned feelings (விலைமாதர் பாவகங்கள்) in which he sinks. Kural 911 says the sweet words (இன்சொல்) of women who desire wealth and not love bring harm. The song spreads into a catalogue the charm the Kural names in one item, and both rest on the pretence.

702 tells the courtesan's cycle: fixing the price, the bed, then snatching the wealth (உள பொருள் பறித்து), quarrelling and beating the man away (கலகமிட்டு அவர் அகல அடித்தபின்). Naladiyar 377 has the same turn: she licks like a wild cow, takes the wealth from his hand (அவர்கைப் பொருள்கொண்டு) and then balks like a buffalo, and the man who thought her love his is laughed at. 702 adds what the Naladiyar leaves out, the new man taken up with new stories.

source_issues: Song 702 ends with இளைய நாயகனே, not பெருமாளே, and names no shrine except தமனியப்பதி (the golden town); its placement under மாடம்பாக்கம் is not confirmed by the text.
